subject: music
title: Listening Foundations: The MAD TSHIRT Toolkit
welcome_lead: Train your ears using MAD TSHIRT — the toolkit every GCSE listener needs to describe any piece of music.
meta_desc: GCSE Music Listening Adventure 1: foundations of musical analysis using the MAD TSHIRT framework — melody, dynamics, texture and more.
final_note: You can now describe what you hear with confidence and clarity.

walkthroughs.h2: A toolkit for every listening question
walkthroughs.body_html:
Melody, Articulation, Dynamics, Texture, Structure, Harmony, Instrumentation, Rhythm, Tempo. Memorise it!

When the examiner asks 'describe this extract', work through MAD TSHIRT and pick the most striking 3–4 features. You'll never run out of things to say.

Use words like stepwise (conjunct), leaping (disjunct), ascending, descending, narrow range, wide range.

Note any repeated motifs, sequences, or ornaments. Is the melody catchy and singable, or fragmented and angular?

Monophonic: a single melody, no harmony. Homophonic: melody with chordal accompaniment. Polyphonic: two or more independent melodies (think Bach fugue). Heterophonic: the same melody with simultaneous variations.

Texture often changes throughout a piece — listen for thickening and thinning.

mcqs.q: How do you identify a major key from its key signature?
options: It is always C major.
The number of sharps or flats equals the tonic note number.
The last sharp is the leading note (semitone below tonic); the second-to-last flat is the tonic.
Heavy use of electric guitars.

mcqs.q: What is a tone row in serial music?
options: It is always C major.
An ordered series of all 12 chromatic pitches, used as the basis of a piece.
Any sequence of notes a composer chooses.
A row of notes played together as a chord.

mcqs.q: What is characteristic of Baroque music?
options: Continuous bass line, ornamentation, terraced dynamics, and counterpoint.
Simple melodies with piano accompaniment.
Heavy use of electric guitars.
It is always C major.

sequence.def: c.500-1400: plainchant and early polyphony — the earliest era here
c.1400-1600: Palestrina's choral polyphony follows the Medieval era
c.1600-1750: Bach, Handel and Vivaldi; basso continuo and ornamentation
c.1750-1820: Haydn and Mozart; balanced phrases and sonata form
c.1820-1900: Chopin and Wagner; bigger orchestras, more emotion
From 1900: Debussy, Stravinsky and beyond — the latest era here
